title: Narration orients, pictures imply
statement: Let narration and captions give the facts students need, such as who people are and where events happen, and leave what the pictures imply for students to infer.
detail: Early drafts of a Grade 9 unit opening were rejected as childish and dashboard-like; the corrected direction in the 6 October handover makes the pictures dense enough to reward attention, lets students infer meaning from setting, posture, relationships and visual details, and has the narration supply factual orientation without explaining every visual implication (lines 53 and 74). The prototype's short captions name people and places without narrating every implication (`g9/prototypes/review-build/DESIGN.md`, line 5).
against: The handover puts orientation first, which limits what can be left to the pictures: students need to know where the action moves, who is connected to whom, what each rank means and why the promotion matters (line 119). No student has used the finished work, so whether students drew the inferences is unmeasured (`g9/README.md`, line 27).

evidence.quote: The narration supplies the necessary factual orientation and carries the story; it should not explain every visual implication or continuously tell the student what to think.
Let visual details carry implications. Keep factual orientation clear without narrating every inference.
Short captions identify names, roles, and places without narrating every implication.
Factual clarity comes first: students need to know where the action moves, who is connected to whom, what each rank means, and why the promotion matters.
